title: Khanti: the elephant and the arrow
hookLine: the week's two perfections come back, and the sixth arrives
carry: khanti: feel the arrow, keep your footing
tomorrow: what does a prince do when his own father turns on him?
last: SEE CLEARLY · WISE IN ACTION · WHAT IS HAPPENING

cards: Someone can sit perfectly still in a waiting room and be boiling inside. Someone else can be stuck in traffic, talking, shifting gears, and be at ease. From the outside they look reversed.
The Pali word for patience, khanti, is about the inside one. It isn't how still you are. It's what happens in you when something hard arrives and won't hurry, whether it's a person or a pain.

teach.b: Khanti is the sixth of the ten perfections, and it bears two loads: people and pain. The Dhammapada gives it a battlefield picture.
In Max Müller's words: "Silently shall I endure abuse as the elephant in battle endures the arrow sent from the bow: for the world is ill-natured." The elephant isn't pretending nothing hit it.
It feels the arrow and keeps its footing. Notice the verse doesn't ask the elephant to love the arrow, or to pretend there is no battle. That links straight back to this week.
Patience needs wisdom, to see what is actually happening instead of the story about it.
And it needs effort, because holding steady is work, not a nap. Look back across the week and the perfections start to lean on each other.
Seeing clearly, acting wisely, steady effort, and now the steadiness to stay while things are slow or sharp.

how: Buddhists practice khanti in daily life by meeting delays, criticism and pain without striking back, and Dhammapada verses on patience are often recited and taught.

o: staying steady inside when people or pain press
sitting still and silent, whatever you feel
a pause before acting on something you want

games.q: the week's perfections — tap the pairs.

s: patience means looking calm on the outside
khanti is the inside steadiness; you can be still and boiling.
the Dhammapada pictures patience as an elephant enduring arrows
it feels the arrow and keeps its footing.
Mahajanaka swam because the shore was in sight
no shore was in sight; he swam anyway.

games.q: your little sister keeps poking you on a long car ride, with two hours to go. which one is khanti?
o: stay steady inside, and calmly offer a game at the next stop.
sit perfectly still and silent, fuming, until she gives up.
poke back once, hard, so the lesson sticks.
games.why: khanti is the inside steadiness, not a frozen face. the elephant feels the arrow and keeps its footing.

practice: Listen for the most annoying sound around you: a hum, traffic, a neighbor's TV. Don't push it away and don't tune it out. Let it land, like the arrow on the elephant, and stay steady while it goes on.

wordCard.voice: Khanti: patience, the sixth perfection. Bearing people and pain without being knocked off your feet.

orig.note: Pali: patience, forbearance; the sixth perfection. Sanskrit kshanti.

carryVoice: For the road: khanti, patience, where the elephant feels the arrow and keeps its footing. That's the week, done.
